notes.meaning: The queen of Sheba traveled a very long way to see if the stories about Solomon's wisdom were true. She brought a large royal caravan carrying gold, jewels, and rare spices. When she arrived, she asked him difficult questions and riddles to test his understanding.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often note that the queen's visit was likely motivated by trade interests, since Solomon's expanding sea commerce threatened Sheba's ancient overland routes for frankincense and myrrh.

notes.meaning: Solomon answered every question the queen asked him without hesitation. No problem was too deep or difficult for him to explain. His God-given wisdom gave him clear answers for everything she brought up.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often note that the queen's visit was likely motivated by trade interests, since Solomon's expanding sea commerce threatened Sheba's ancient overland routes for frankincense and myrrh.

notes.meaning: The queen looked at Solomon's palace, the banquet food, and the well-ordered way his servants were seated and dressed. She also saw the grand entrance he used to go up to the Lord's temple. The sheer beauty and order of everything left her completely breathless.

The queen confessed to the king that the glowing reports she had heard back home were completely true. She had doubted the news at first, but seeing his wisdom and wealth with her own eyes proved it was far greater than she had been told. The original reports had not captured even half of his greatness.

The queen declared that Solomon's servants and officials were truly blessed. They enjoyed the special privilege of being in his presence every day and listening to his wise words. Their daily joy showed how good it was to live under a wise and caring ruler.

The queen praised the Lord for choosing Solomon and setting him on Israel's throne. She recognized that Solomon ruled as God's representative because God loved His people and wanted to establish them in justice. True leaders receive their authority from God to do what is right.

differ.view: The queen's praise shows God's ancient promise to Abraham being fulfilled, as foreign nations began to encounter and bless the God of Israel.
Her words may have been polite royal courtesy rather than a genuine personal conversion to faith in Israel's God.

notes.meaning: She presented Solomon with over four tons of gold, along with precious stones and vast stores of spices. Her gift of perfumes and sweet spices like myrrh was greater than anything Jerusalem had ever seen before. These treasures showed how deeply she respected Solomon and his God.

The trading ships of King Hiram and Solomon brought back fine timber called algum wood from Ophir, along with gold and jewels. Solomon used this rare wood to build walkways and steps for the temple and palace, and to make harps and lyres for the singers. Nothing like these fine instruments and woodwork had ever been seen in Judah.

Solomon generously gave the queen of Sheba everything she requested, even exceeding what she had brought to him. He showered her with royal gifts before she packed up her caravan and traveled back to her own country. God's generosity often flows through the hands of His people.

Solomon collected about twenty-five tons of gold every single year. On top of this regular income, he received taxes from traveling traders and tribute gifts of gold and silver from Arabian kings and local governors. His kingdom reached an unmatched level of material wealth.

differ.view: The yearly sum of 666 talents of gold signals a subtle warning of spiritual decay, linking excessive wealth to human pride and the later beast of Revelation.

notes.meaning: Solomon made two hundred large shields and three hundred smaller shields out of hammered gold. These dazzling gold shields were not meant for real warfare, but were displayed by royal guards in the hall known as the House of the Forest of Lebanon. They put the glory and wealth of his kingdom on public display.

Solomon constructed a magnificent royal throne out of ivory and plated it with pure gold. It had six steps with a golden footstool, armrests flanked by two carved lions, and twelve more lions standing at the ends of the steps. No other nation in the ancient world possessed a seat of judgment so grand.

Every royal cup Solomon drank from was made of pure gold, as were all the dishes used in his forest palace. Gold was so common that silver was treated as having little value. God fulfilled His promise to give Solomon riches beyond any other king.

Solomon owned a fleet of large cargo ships that sailed on long voyages with Hiram's Phoenician sailors. Every three years the ships returned to port carrying gold, silver, ivory, and exotic animals like apes and baboons or peacocks. These goods showed how far Israel's trading reach stretched across the seas.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars debate whether the ships sailed west toward Tartessus in Spain or south through the Red Sea to East Africa or Arabia, with 'ships of Tarshish' likely naming large, ocean-going vessels.

notes.meaning: Solomon stood far above every other king in the known world in both riches and wisdom. His prosperity matched his mental brilliance, proving that God had kept His word to bless him richly. His peaceful reign was a golden age for the nation.

Kings from all over the region came to Jerusalem to hear the wisdom God had placed in Solomon's heart. Year after year, these visiting rulers brought tribute gifts of silver, gold, fine robes, armor, spices, horses, and mules. In this way, Solomon pointed the surrounding nations toward the true God who gave him understanding.

Solomon maintained four thousand stalls for his chariot horses, along with twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed these forces partly in special chariot cities across the land and partly with himself in Jerusalem. This large military network kept peace throughout his borders.

Solomon ruled over all the smaller kingdoms from the Euphrates River in the north to the Philistine coast and down to the border of Egypt. The kings in these regions paid him regular tribute and lived in submission to him. This vast territory marked the widest reach the nation of Israel ever held.

Wealth was so widespread during Solomon's reign that silver in Jerusalem became as common as ordinary rocks. Valuable cedar logs from Lebanon were as plentiful as the common fig trees that grew in the low hills. The abundance reflected God's generous hand upon the nation.

differ.view: Multiplying horses from Egypt was an explicit breach of Deuteronomy 17:16, warning readers of the quiet beginnings of Solomon's compromise.

notes.meaning: Solomon imported fine horses from Egypt and other surrounding lands to build up his forces and trade. He turned Israel into a central trading hub for horses and chariots across the ancient Near East. This trade network added even more wealth to his crown.

differ.view: Multiplying horses from Egypt was an explicit breach of Deuteronomy 17:16, warning readers of the quiet beginnings of Solomon's compromise.

notes.meaning: The full story of Solomon's life was recorded by the prophets Nathan, Ahijah, and Iddo the seer. These prophetic histories provided detailed records of his words and royal deeds, though the original books are no longer around today. The biblical writer drew on these trustworthy records to remind God's people of their heritage.

Solomon reigned over a united Israel from Jerusalem for forty years. His four decades on the throne were marked by peace, magnificent building projects, and broad international renown. It was the only time in biblical history when the twelve tribes enjoyed such prolonged unity and wealth.

differ.view: The Chronicler's total silence about Solomon's late-life idolatry suggests that he repented before death and was pardoned by God.
The phrase 'rested with his fathers' is used of both wicked and godly kings, leaving Solomon's eternal standing uncertain after his tragic fall into idolatry.

notes.meaning: Solomon died and was buried in Jerusalem, the city named after his father David. His son Rehoboam then took the throne in his place. Even the greatest earthly king must eventually face death, leaving his kingdom to the next generation.
